thread.title: Why The Shorts Get Burned: Tesla And The Theory Of Reflexivity - Tesla, Inc. (NASDAQ:TSLA)

author: MacGregor Ross
title: Why The Shorts Get Burned: Tesla And The Theory Of Reflexivity - Tesla, Inc. (NASDAQ:TSLA)
text:
Introduction For the purposes of intellectual curiosity, there has been no stock on the market that has captured my interest like Tesla, Inc. ( TSLA ). To understand why, I would implore readers to take a brief glance at the recent headlines of analyst articles. One will find an unbelievably diverse set of opinions, from bulls calling for prices as high as the moon, to bears declaring imminent and utter bankruptcy, and everything in-between.
Part of my interest has also been driven by Tesla's eventful year. The stock has been extremely volatile for a large cap: share prices have bounced around, having taken a hit of ~20% earlier in the year (from $320 to a nadir of $250), only to enjoy a subsequent rally back to the $300-plus level as of yesterday.
The initial decline was not without reason. There have been a number of bumps in the road lately, from the failed Model 3 production targets to the famous " earnings call debacle ". The company also continues to burn through cash at an unprecedented rate while remaining unprofitable, giving rise to serious liquidity concerns - so much so that it caused Moody's to downgrade Tesla's already lackluster debt rating. These issues have culminated in the company recently regaining its position as the most shorted stock in the US market.
The bearish thesis is obvious - short sellers doubt Tesla's ability to control costs and become profitable. But this begs the question, what could the bullish thesis possibly be? What rationale could be used to justify a $300 share price for a company plagued with such complications?
The answer is narrative.
It is the story of Tesla and its CEO, Elon Musk, that drives the bullish position. A technology company poised to dominate every facet of the rapidly expanding electric vehicle market, led by a young business visionary. Musk offers bulls a chance to join in on a meteoric ascension along the likes of Steve Jobs with Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL ), or Jeff Bezos with Amazon (NASDAQ: AMZN ). Tesla and its leader aspire to reach great heights, and the return on investment promises to be exceptional if those heights are reached. Now, that's one hell of a story.
Short sellers have to face the facts: they have been consistently burned by Musk and his company's narrative. The potential collapse that is suggested by the poor financial picture has, at least for now, been avoided. That being said, the great disconnect remains: Tesla's financials do not match up to its current share price. But, how has this situation persisted, and, more importantly, for how long can the disconnect continue?
I believe the answers to these questions can be explained by "reflexivity" - a socio-economic theory developed by legendary investor George Soros. But before introducing this theory and its relation to Tesla, it is first necessary to lay out both the objective bearish financial reality and subjective bullish narrative for the company.
Tesla's Bearish Case - Understanding Financial Reality To gain an understanding of the bearish perspective on Tesla, one need look no further than the company's financials. By any traditional method of valuation, be it comparative or cash flow, the company is dramatically overvalued.
Some excellent valuation work on Tesla has been conducted by Professor Aswath Damodaran, a finance professor at NYU who has followed the company closely for a number of years. Damodaran has published a number of valuation articles covering Tesla, as well as a free-use financial model on his blog, "Musings on Markets" . Given his last update was in August of 2017, I will be updating some of the model's numbers and presenting the case that a $300+ share price is absurd.
On a comparative basis, Tesla's financial metrics are outright dismal compared to other automotive competitors. These are the sorts of numbers that could only be attributed to an overvalued growth stock:
Source: Author created using Damodaran's template from 2017
Despite having less than 10% and 2% of Ford's (NYSE: F ) revenues and cars sold in 2017, as well as a negative EBITDA, shareholders still value Tesla higher than Ford. A situation like this is surreal: investors would pay more for the non-existent earnings of a speculative automotive company, rather than immediately own the substantial and already-established earnings of Ford.
Bulls would take issue with the statement above - the idea is that Tesla is going to overthrow the Fords of the world, giving its earnings potential meaningful upside. But how many things need to go right for that potential to become a reality?
That question can be answered in part by turning to a cash flow basis of valuation. In his August article, Professor Damodaran estimated the company's value to be worth somewhere around $192 per share. I imagine that figure would be somewhat lower given the recent developments with the company, as well as a larger number of outstanding shares.
Bulls might criticize Damodaran's $192 per share valuation for being overly pessimistic about the time it takes Tesla to generate a profit. The model assumes six years until a positive EBIT, which is longer than most analysts expect it will take. However, if we take the model and perform sensitivity analysis on his initial estimate by manipulating a number of variables, the bullish counter-argument of Tesla's potential still seems ludicrous:
Source: Author created using Damodaran's Tesla model. RG = Revenue Growth
Based on my assumptions (all of which are bullish), there are a very limited number of scenarios that could result in Tesla's current share prices being undervalued. Generally, they involve ten years of annual revenue growth north of 50%, as well as a 12% operating margin.
Assumptions such as these need some serious perspective. A 50% annual revenue growth for ten years is virtually unheard of in business - not even Apple from 2005 to 2015 could outpace that growth. It would result in Tesla's annual revenues growing to ~$250 billion, becoming one of the largest car companies in the world only behind the likes of Volkswagen ( OTCPK:VLKAF ) and Toyota (NYSE: TM ) (based on current figures). Not only that, but a 12% EBIT - twice the industry average - that becomes positive by the end of next year is the absolute best case for Tesla. Not even the most bullish of analysts would believe this to be a probability, in light of the ongoing issues and the company's historical inability to turn an operating profit in over ten years of business.
At the best-case scenario of $560 NPV per share, the question needs to be asked: if this growth stock can only offer an upside of ~87%, is it worth the risk? Because even slight downward adjustments to the optimistic assumptions from non-extraordinary levels show extreme downside risk. Take the still bullish example of 10% revenue growth paired with a 12% positive EBIT by 2019, and no reinvestment costs to boot. NPV per share is estimated at a mere $31, a tenth of current share prices. Other assumptions, still bullish in nature, also lead to a result that depicts current share prices to be overvalued. I encourage both bulls and bears to play around with Damodaran's model and test the results for themselves.
Of other significance is the fact that the model doesn't significantly account for potential volatility in capital markets, something that would seriously damage the cycle-sensitive auto industry, Tesla included. Vocal bear James Chanos, President of Kynikos Associates, pointed this out (among other things):
“Put it this way,” Chanos said. “If you wouldn’t be short a multi-billion-dollar loss-making enterprise in a cyclical business, with a leveraged balance sheet, questionable accounting, every executive leaving, run by a CEO with a questionable relationship with the truth, what would you be short? It sort of ticks all the boxes.”
Source: Reuters
In conclusion, even if we take the most conservative of scenarios for the bearish position and ignore the risk of a market correction, Tesla is either dramatically overvalued or at the very least holds limited upside. The bearish thesis appears to carry legitimacy.
Tesla's Bullish Case - Narrative and Reflexivity Theory But this brings us back to the original question: why is Tesla's share price moving away from its apparent financial equilibrium? Why do the shorts keep getting burned?
Perhaps it is because they are only seeing half the picture.
For any given investment, there exist two domains that have an influence on price. First, the financial reality; and second, the narrative surrounding that investment. The financial reality is an objective fact and acts as a tether to an investment's narrative. The narrative, conversely, is subjective and is responsible for bringing prices to levels above or below the objective financial equilibrium.
Elon Musk has woven a compelling narrative that inspires bulls to believe in the transformative power of him and his company. Tesla is at the forefront of a possible revolution, one in which it changes the world by capturing the rapidly growing electric vehicle market. This revolution has dramatic implications for a number of existential issues for humanity, namely sustainable development, artificial intelligence, and climate change. Tesla also promises to bring investors along for a profitable ride behind one of the latest uber-successful business visionaries in Musk. If recent history is any indicator, you want to be on the same team as the visionaries - people who are capable of overcoming incredible odds to change the world.
Surely, the Tesla shorts are aware of this narrative. Any rational bear understands that Musk at the very least has the possibility for transcendent accomplishments with his company. Rather, they would likely make the case that the dichotomy between the objective financial reality and the subjective narrative is too severe for him to overcome. And perhaps rightly so.
But even if the bearish thesis for Tesla is justified, the short position isn't necessarily so. This may seem bizarre to short sellers - if the objective reality of Tesla's financials is bearish, how could a short position not be an intelligent investment strategy?
This is where "reflexivity theory" comes into play. Reflexivity theory was first developed by legendary investor George Soros, who has cited it as a primary reason for his astounding success in financial markets. Loosely defined, reflexivity refers to the ability of human subjective interpretation to transform an underlying objective reality. This transformation of the underlying reality then "reflexively" adjusts subjective interpretations, leading to further transformations of reality, and so forth. This brings about a continuous feedback loop; in other words, a self-fulfilling prophecy.
A simple example from Wikipedia helps to illustrate this phenomenon:
An example Soros cites is the procyclical nature of lending, that is, the willingness of banks to ease lending standards for real estate loans when prices are rising, then raising standards when real estate prices are falling, reinforcing the boom and bust cycle.
Banks are more willing to lend more money in times of rising real-estate prices, which serves to raise real-estate prices, which causes banks to lend more money.
In short: expectations alter reality, which circularly alters expectations.
Thus, when one considers reflexivity theory in relation to Tesla, the long history of short sellers losing big starts to make sense. Tesla's extremely compelling narrative (subjective expectations) driven by Musk and his supporters has propelled share prices (objective reality) to great heights, which has served to legitimize the narrative, further raising share prices, etc. It is a feedback loop in which short sellers are necessarily destined to lose - until they don't.
One might consider this scenario as that of a typical bubble, but this isn't exactly the case. Tesla's rising share prices have had a real-world impact on its ability to mature into the narrative that surrounds it. One example would be the company's greatly improved ability to raise capital: Tesla is expected to have substantial liquidity requirements in the coming years for a number of new projects, but this won't be a significant obstacle to growth given current share prices.
Another example is the company's ability to generate sales with virtually no marketing, an impressive feat that is solely a consequence of its story. This advantage was part of the rationale for the recent $2 billion SolarCity acquisition. The company has the power to cut the fat from SolarCity's budget by eliminating significant marketing and sales expenses by simply selling the product in existing Tesla stores, where products seem to market themselves. This incredible brand power paired with SolarCity's integration potential with Tesla as a whole lends some financial credibility to the acquisition, which has been questioned by some as lacking integrity.
A single, critical question remains: what could put an end to this reflexivity loop? That's an interesting question that lacks a definitive answer. In all likelihood, it will take a significant event or failure of some kind. This could take form in a major broken promise (though this hasn't stopped Elon yet), or a substantial correction in financial markets. But, ultimately, short sellers would be speculating on the timing of when something like that happens - and speculations rarely, if ever, make quality investments.
Conclusion In conclusion, Tesla represents a fascinating investment case. On the one hand, there exists the bearish thesis: that the company's objective financial reality implies current share prices are dramatically overvalued. And, on the other, there exists the bullish thesis: that Elon Musk and Tesla operate within a subjective narrative that presents investors the opportunity to transform the world and defy traditional metrics of valuation.
This narrative has served to create a bullish reflexive feedback loop that improves both share prices and the objective financial reality in which Tesla exists. Short sellers have historically been burned by this reflexive loop and should expect to continue to lose on their positions until some form of black-swan event takes place, snapping the company and its share prices out of the cycle.
Disclosure: I/we have no positions in any stocks mentioned, and no plans to initiate any positions within the next 72 hours.
